headline: Amateur Researcher Maps All Omnicorp Properties, Claims to Find 'Geometric Pattern'
subheadline: 47 properties across the city form shape that 'shouldn't be possible,' researcher says before scrubbing all social media
summary: A local data analyst spent eight months mapping every property owned by Omnicorp Holdings, discovering a pattern she now refuses to discuss.
content:
Lisa Huang spent eight months compiling public records, property deeds, and corporate filings to create what she called "the definitive map of Omnicorp Holdings' real estate portfolio." She posted her findings to Threadit last week. The post was deleted within hours, and Huang has since deactivated all social media accounts.

Before the deletion, several users archived her work.

Huang identified 47 properties owned directly by Omnicorp or through subsidiary shell companies. These include the Hartwell Building, three office parks, a water treatment facility, two cell phone towers, and 40 residential properties scattered across the city.

"When you plot them on a map, they form a shape," Huang wrote in her original post. "At first I thought it was coincidence. Then I measured the distances. Each property is exactly 847 meters from at least two other Omnicorp properties. Exactly. To the centimeter."

The shape, according to cached images, appears to be a series of interconnected triangles forming a larger geometric pattern. Huang noted that the Hartwell Building sits at the precise center.

"I showed this to a mathematician friend," Huang continued. "He said the geometry was 'non-Euclidean.' I asked what that meant. He said it meant the pattern works on paper but shouldn't work in physical space. He stopped returning my calls after that."

Omnicorp Holdings declined to comment on the property map, stating only that their "real estate portfolio reflects strategic business decisions made over many decades."

Efforts to reach Huang have been unsuccessful. Her former employer, a local accounting firm, confirmed she resigned last week "to pursue personal interests." A neighbor reported seeing her leave her apartment with a single suitcase, saying only that she was "going somewhere they can't draw lines."

Dr. Elena Martinez of the local university's physics department was shown the archived map. She studied it for several minutes before handing it back.

"I'm a physicist, not a geometer," she said. "But I will say this: there are shapes that exist in mathematics that we don't expect to find in the physical world. When we do find them, it usually means someone put them there on purpose." She declined further comment.

The cached version of Huang's map has been viewed 84,700 times. Threadit moderators have not explained why the original post was removed.
author: Tom Hendricks, City Hall Reporter
